title: Arrays, objects, immutability
blurb: Copying, mutation, array methods, Map and Set. The material behind every 'why did unrelated state change?' bug.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: Spread is a shallow copy: `b.user` and `a.user` are the same object. For a real copy use structuredClone(a), or copy each level you intend to change.
questions.asked: This is the React state bug in its purest form.

questions.q: Which produces a new array with an item replaced at index 2, without mutating?
questions.why: map returns a new array. Direct assignment, splice and fill all mutate in place — fine for a local array, wrong for anything held as state. Modern engines also offer `items.with(2, next)`.

questions.q: What does `reduce` do?
choices: Folds an array into a single accumulated value
Removes elements that fail a test
Shortens the array to a fixed length
questions.why: reduce((acc, item) => next, initial). It can express map and filter, but if a map or filter says it more clearly, use those instead — readability is the whole point.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually 'implement groupBy with reduce'.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: The arrow has a block body with no return, so every callback returns undefined. Removing the braces (or adding `return`) fixes it.

questions.q: How do you deduplicate an array of primitives?
questions.why: Set keeps insertion order and uses SameValueZero equality. It does not deduplicate objects with equal contents — those are different references, so you need a key function.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.code:
const set = new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]);
console.log(set.size);
questions.why: Set compares by reference for objects. Two structurally identical literals are different objects. Deduplicate by a key: build a Map keyed on item.id.
questions.asked: The natural follow-up to the dedupe question, and it catches a lot of people.

questions.q: What is the difference between `find` and `filter`?
choices: find returns the first matching element or undefined; filter returns an array of all matches
find works on objects, filter on arrays
questions.why: find short-circuits on the first hit. Using `filter(...)[0]` works but scans the whole array and allocates an array you throw away.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: Integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order. This is why you cannot rely on an object to preserve an arbitrary order — use a Map or an array.
questions.asked: It comes up when someone stores an ordered list in an object keyed by id and the order changes.

questions.q: How do you safely check whether an object has its own property `key`?
choices: `obj.hasOwnProperty` called directly on a possibly-null-prototype object
questions.why: `in` also finds inherited properties. Checking against undefined cannot distinguish a missing key from one explicitly set to undefined. Object.hasOwn works even on objects created with a null prototype.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: `__proto__` is an accessor on Object.prototype: assigning a number to it is ignored, and reading it returns the prototype. Counting user-supplied words in a plain object is therefore a real bug — use a Map or Object.create(null).
questions.asked: It is the concrete reason 'use a Map for a lookup keyed by user input' is real advice, not style.

questions.q: What does `array.flatMap(fn)` do?
choices: Maps then flattens one level — useful for map-and-filter in one pass
questions.why: Returning `[]` from the callback drops the element and returning `[value]` keeps it, so flatMap expresses 'map some, skip others' without two passes.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: length is writable — shrinking it truncates the array in place. Growing it creates holes, which most array methods skip rather than visit.

questions.q: Which is the correct immutable way to add an item to the front of an array?
questions.why: unshift and splice mutate. concat appends to the end. Spread with the new item first builds a fresh array in the right order.

questions.q: What is wrong with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` as a deep clone?
choices: It loses Dates, Maps, Sets, undefined, functions, and throws on cycles
Nothing — it is the recommended approach
questions.why: Dates become strings, undefined-valued keys vanish, Map/Set become {}, and a circular reference throws. `structuredClone` handles all of those (though still not functions).
questions.asked: Everyone has used this trick; the question is whether you know its limits.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to itself. indexOf uses strict equality, and NaN !== NaN, so it can never find one.

questions.q: How do you group an array of objects by a field?
choices: `Object.groupBy(items, (item) => item.type)` — or a reduce into a Map
questions.why: Object.groupBy (and Map.groupBy) are the modern built-ins. Before them the idiom was a reduce that pushes into `acc[key] ??= []` — worth being able to write from memory.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Object.entries` and `Object.getOwnPropertyNames`?
choices: entries gives enumerable string-keyed pairs; getOwnPropertyNames includes non-enumerable keys
questions.why: Both look only at own properties, but entries skips non-enumerable ones and returns [key, value] pairs. Neither sees symbol keys.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: sort mutates and returns the same array reference. So `const sorted = state.sort()` mutates your state and hands you the same object back — which React will then think is unchanged.
questions.asked: A great one-liner for testing whether someone understands referential equality.

questions.q: When would you use a `WeakMap` over a `Map`?
choices: To attach data to objects without preventing them from being garbage collected
When you need it to be faster
When you need to iterate the entries
questions.why: WeakMap holds keys weakly, so an entry disappears when nothing else references the key object. That is why it cannot be iterated or sized — and why it is right for caches and private data keyed by instance.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: map creates a new array but copies the same references into it. To copy each row too: `rows.map((row) => ({ ...row }))`.
questions.asked: The 'I did copy it' bug — the array is new, the contents are not.

questions.q: What is the result?
questions.code:
console.log([1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b));
console.log([].reduce((a, b) => a + b));
questions.why: reduce with no initial value on an empty array throws 'Reduce of empty array with no initial value'. Always pass the initial value — it also fixes the type when the accumulator differs from the elements.

questions.q: Which comparison correctly sorts objects by a date field, newest first?
choices: `items.sort((a, b) => b.date - a.date)` with Date values
questions.why: A comparator must return a number: negative, zero or positive. Returning a boolean coerces to 0 or 1 and never says 'a before b', so the sort is unstable garbage. Dates subtract cleanly because they coerce to timestamps.
questions.asked: Returning a boolean from a comparator is a surprisingly common bug that mostly works on small arrays.

questions.q: What does destructuring with a rest element do?
choices: rest is a new object { a: 2, b: 3 } — a shallow copy without id
questions.why: This is the idiomatic 'omit a key' operation, and it is also how React components forward unknown props: `const { className, ...rest } = props`.

questions.q: Why can two structurally identical objects fail an equality check?
questions.why: Every object literal creates a new reference. Comparing contents means writing a deep-equal, or comparing a canonical key. This is also why an inline object as a React dependency re-triggers an effect on every render.
questions.asked: It links directly to the React useEffect dependency question.
